Each item below is a decision point in an AI-safety research project. You get the kind of decision, a short statement of the problem the team faced, and the text of their write-up that comes BEFORE the decision. You do not see what they decided, and you must not guess it.

For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "question": str}]}

Readers who knew what the team decided found that this version steers toward one particular resolution: it states or implies it, mentions elements that only one resolution would use, or frames the question so that one resolution is the obvious answer. You are still not told the decision. Rewrite the context and question so that several genuinely different resolutions answer the question equally directly: keep the facts any option needs, present facts that cut different ways neutrally, drop details that only matter to one particular resolution, and invent nothing.

Potential Biases ---------------- Effective Altruists are unfortunately not immune to biases, some of which we want to highlight. However, we think that the founding process, discussions with other EAs, and input from funders should mitigate these biases a lot. Therefore, we think these biases are much less important than the considerations above. 1. **Money:** There is a lot of money in AI. EAs are not immune to the desire to be rich. However, most money comes from improving the state-of-the-art and much less from safety work - at least for now. 2. **Rationalization:** It’s easy to say that “someone else would have found the new technique if I didn’t” and it’s hard or impossible to evaluate this counterfactual. 3. **Tired of being pessimistic about the future:** Some EAs might be sick of being the bad messenger all the time. The message “I think AI is good, we just need to make it safe” gives you much more pleasurable human interactions than “You’re gonna kill us all. Stop doing the thing that might make you rich”. Conclusion ---------- Our main goal with this post is to highlight different considerations on AI acceleration in AI safety research. Broadly, we think that view 1 (no-acceleration) would be the default if everyone in AI worked on alignment. Views 2 (side-effects) and 3 (control) come from the interaction with non-aligned actors, e.g. since other actors continually increase state of the art, the safety community has sometimes to make decisions that could accelerate AI.
Previous context: A research team wrote an analysis laying out three broad views on whether AI-safety work should ever accelerate AI capabilities: never accelerate, accelerate only for beneficial side-effects, or accelerate when it improves control or leverage. They catalogued considerations favoring each view, plus potential biases (money, rationalization, fatigue with pessimism) that they judge less important than the substantive considerations. They now need to write a conclusion that characterizes how the views relate without overstating what the analysis establishes.
Previous question: How strongly should the team state which of the three views on AI acceleration is correct?

LLM-Graded Quality Score ------------------------ We created an LLM judge to grade the quality score of eval questions by putting together a scoring rubric and few-shot examples (see Appendix D for full prompt). **“Quality” refers to relevance to the harmful behavior being evaluated, the absence of confounders, correctly labeled answer choices, and correspondence to answers that reflect the harmful behavior** (as opposed to simply stated preferences). We defined the rubric in a way that spells out the criteria for each score separately (between 1 and 10), to encourage higher self-consistency. We also provided 12 few-shot examples (as user and assistant turns) with a variety of eval questions and scores to leverage in-context learning capabilities. We ran the judge on all 24.5k evals in the datasets, along with the 160 few-shot examples the Anthropic researchers wrote to prompt the LLMs when generating the MWEs. [Research has shown](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13076v1) LLM evaluators tend to favor their own generations (Panickssery et al., 2024), [...] (pre-release Claude 1 for the original dataset and Claude 3.5-Sonnet for our new one). Finally, we spot-checked a random sample of the graded evals and refined the prompt to resolve any apparent inaccuracies. When generating new eval datasets, we ran the quality scoring on each batch of questions.

=== key 44edcffa028e

Problem: How strongly to state conclusions about the diversity metrics
Write-up text before the decision: work on this approach would include automating the prompt optimization method and using an LLM to review the flagged eval questions, then rewrite and retest them to check if they can elicit different responses. Dataset Diversity Metrics ------------------------- With the input space for LLMs being so large, an ongoing challenge with evals is knowing how much “test coverage” a given dataset possesses. This is partially addressed by adding variant prompts, generating hundreds of questions, and using visualization techniques like UMAP. However, we want a quantitative way to know whether an eval dataset is becoming more or less diverse. This can help benchmark developers understand if generating additional questions is adding more test coverage for the various topics/semantics/phrasings for eval questions. We contribute two novel metrics to compute how widely spread and how evenly distributed an eval dataset is in a high-dimensional embedding space. We care about the spread because it means the dataset covers a wide range of topics, semantics, and other features represented in the embedding space. We also care about an even distribution of points within that space because it means we aren’t missing any large regimes of coverage due to most of the questions being concentrated in a small subspace. While these metrics have some limitations and are sensitive to the embedding model chosen, we think it’s a helpful heuristic to use in the eval generation process to know at a glance if diversity is improving. *Disclaimer: These metrics are a first attempt to formalize coverage.
Previous context: A research team developing tools for LLM evaluation wanted a quantitative way to judge how much 'test coverage' an eval dataset has, beyond adding variant prompts and using visualizations. They computed two metrics capturing how widely spread and how evenly distributed a dataset's questions are in a high-dimensional embedding space. They knew the metrics were sensitive to the choice of embedding model and had other limitations.

Introduction ============ We think that the quality of causal world models of LLMs matters for AI safety and alignment. More capable LLMs are supposed to assist humans in important decisions and solve scientific questions. For all of these applications, it is important that their causal world model is accurate, i.e. that they accurately reflect the causal relationships of the real world. For a more detailed motivation, see [this AF post](/api/post/oqzasmQ9Lye45QDMZ). In this post, we will investigate these causal relationships in multiple simple real-world and toy data settings. One question that we are specifically interested in is whether the LLM bases its answer primarily on the form of the sentence or on its content. For example, does the order of presenting facts matter for the end result when the content stays the same? *We will use the word “understanding” in the context of LLMs because it leads to a better reading flow than “can recreate a pattern” or similar. However, we don’t make any claims about whether the model “truly understands” a phenomenon or the nature of understanding.* ### Meta Originally, we wanted this project to have two parts, one that treats the LLM as a black box and only looks at input-output behavior, and another part in which we open the black box with different interpretability techniques. However, during the course of the project, it became clear that only the most capable model (i.e. the best GPT-3 version) is able to consistently solve even our simplest problems.
Previous context: A research team is studying whether large language models have accurate causal world models, focusing on whether the model's answers depend on the form of a prompt or its content. They had planned a two-part project: black-box input-output experiments plus interpretability analysis inside the model. Partway through, they found that only the most capable model could consistently solve even their simplest tasks.
Previous question: Should the team keep the planned two-part design or restrict the project to black-box testing?
